title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 15
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A swimming pool introduced small-group lessons in place of individual ones and reports that the proportion of children passing the beginner assessment rose. It concludes that small groups teach beginners better than one-to-one instruction.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Small-group lessons cost parents less.
B. Some instructors prefer teaching groups.
C. Individual lessons remain available on request.
D. The pool's changing rooms were refurbished.
E. The pool simultaneously lowered the standard required to pass the beginner assessment.
questions.explanation: If the threshold moved, the pass rate says nothing about teaching; the measure and the standard changed together.

questions.prompt: A tyre manufacturer reports that drivers who fit its winter tyres have fewer accidents in winter than drivers who do not, and advertises the tyres as making winter driving safer.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the advertisement?
options: A. Drivers who buy winter tyres are those most concerned about winter conditions, and they also drive less in bad weather and at lower speeds.
B. Winter tyres wear faster in warm weather.
C. The tyres are more expensive than standard tyres.
D. Some countries require winter tyres by law.
E. Accident rates rise in winter generally.
questions.explanation: The purchasers differ in behaviour as well as equipment, so the accident gap need owe nothing to the tyres themselves.

questions.prompt: A charity sent two versions of a fundraising letter and found that the version mentioning a specific named beneficiary raised more per letter than the version citing statistics on the scale of need. It concludes that donors respond better to individual stories.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating that conclusion?
options: A. How much the letters cost to print
B. Whether the named beneficiary consented
C. Whether the two versions were sent to comparable groups of recipients
D. How many recipients read the letter fully
E. Whether the charity has used statistics before
questions.explanation: If the mailing lists differed in wealth or prior giving, the comparison is between audiences rather than between letters. C is an ethical question that does not bear on the inference.

questions.prompt: A hotel began including breakfast in its room rate and reports that guests now rate value for money more highly, although the total price they pay is unchanged.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, best explains this result?
options: A. Breakfast is served until eleven.
B. The hotel employs additional kitchen staff.
C. Some guests eat breakfast elsewhere.
D. Guests who previously skipped the separately priced breakfast now consume it, so they receive more for the same outlay.
E. Room rates at competing hotels have risen.
questions.explanation: The bundle changes what is actually consumed, so value received rises even though the price does not — no perceptual explanation is required.

questions.prompt: Every freight service on the Kentmere line that runs overnight is hauled by the operator's newest locomotives. No service hauled by the newest locomotives has been cancelled for mechanical failure this year. Some freight services on the line have been cancelled for mechanical failure.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. The newest locomotives are more reliable than the older ones.
B. Some freight services on the line do not run overnight.
C. Most services on the line run overnight.
D. No overnight service has ever been cancelled.
E. Older locomotives are used only in daytime.
questions.explanation: Cancelled services were not hauled by the newest locomotives, and overnight running implies those locomotives, so the cancelled services were not overnight ones. B is a causal reading the statements do not establish.

questions.prompt: A farm invested in robotic weeding equipment and reports that its herbicide use has fallen by 70 per cent, presenting this as evidence that the robots have reduced the farm's environmental impact.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating that presentation?
options: A. How much the robots cost to purchase
B. Whether neighbouring farms have adopted similar equipment
C. How many hours the robots operate each day
D. Whether the robots' manufacture, energy use and soil compaction offset the reduction in herbicide
E. Whether the farm's yields have changed
questions.explanation: A claim about overall impact requires the whole balance, not one input; the substituted burdens may be smaller, larger or simply different in kind.

questions.prompt: An online shoe retailer found that customers who read its sizing guide return fewer pairs than customers who do not, and plans to require every customer to view the guide before ordering.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. The guide takes two minutes to read.
B. Customers who consult the guide are those already uncertain about size, and their return rate is low because they order carefully in other ways too.
C. Some customers order two sizes deliberately.
D. Returns are free.
E. The guide is available in several languages.
questions.explanation: Consulting the guide marks a careful buyer rather than creating one, so compelling everyone to view it need not lower returns.

questions.prompt: A dental service reports that patients who attend check-ups twice a year need fewer fillings than patients who attend annually, and proposes recommending six-monthly check-ups to all patients.
questions.question: The proposal assumes which of the following?
options: A. Six-monthly attendance is affordable for all patients.
B. Fillings are the main outcome of dental care.
C. Dentists have capacity for additional appointments.
D. Patients report their attendance accurately.
E. The difference in fillings reflects the frequency of attendance rather than differences between the patients who choose each interval.
questions.explanation: The recommendation extends a comparison between self-selected groups to everyone, which requires that the interval, not the patient, be doing the work. D is a capacity constraint rather than a premise of the inference.

questions.prompt: A streaming service raised its monthly price and reports that revenue rose in the following quarter. It concludes that it could raise the price again with a similar result.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Subscribers are billed monthly.
B. The service added new programmes in the same quarter.
C. Most subscribers are on annual plans whose prices have not yet been affected, and cancellations among monthly subscribers were high.
D. Competing services charge more.
E. Some subscribers share accounts.
questions.explanation: The quarter's revenue conceals the response, since most subscribers have not yet faced the higher price and those who did left in numbers. C offers a rival cause but does not show the inference to be unsafe on its own terms.

questions.prompt: A city refurbished a playground and reports that the number of children using the park has risen. A councillor argues that refurbishing the other playgrounds in the city would produce similar increases everywhere.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the councillor's argument?
options: A. Attendance at the two nearest playgrounds fell by a combined amount close to the increase.
B. The refurbishment took three months.
C. The refurbished playground has new climbing equipment.
D. The city has twelve playgrounds.
E. Parents were consulted about the design.
questions.explanation: The gain appears to be redistribution between sites; refurbishing all of them cannot repeat an effect that consisted of drawing users from elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A health agency argues that a new vaccine will substantially reduce disease in a rural region, citing trial results showing 85 per cent efficacy. A critic notes that the vaccine must be kept below a temperature that the region's clinics cannot currently maintain.
questions.question: The critic's point weakens the agency's argument by
options: A. disputing the trial's efficacy figure
B. identifying a condition on which the trial result depends and which does not hold in the setting under discussion
C. arguing that the disease is less common than reported
D. questioning the ethics of the trial
E. proposing a different vaccine
questions.explanation: Efficacy under trial conditions transfers only if the conditions transfer; a broken cold chain means the product delivered is not the product tested.

questions.passageText:
Family-controlled firms are often treated as a transitional form that professional management eventually replaces. They remain a large share of enterprises in every economy that has been measured, including the most developed, and the persistence is not explained by inertia alone.

Family control resolves one problem cheaply. Where ownership is dispersed, shareholders must monitor managers who spend their money, and the mechanisms for doing so — boards, disclosure, takeover threats — are expensive and imperfect. An owner who also manages needs no such apparatus. Family firms also tend to hold longer horizons, because the owners expect to hand the business on rather than to sell at the next peak, and they sustain relationships with employees and suppliers that survive downturns in ways a firm managed to quarterly results often cannot.

The costs appear at succession. The pool of candidates in one family is small, and the evidence that firms passing control to a family heir underperform those recruiting outside is among the more consistent findings in the field. A family may also extract value in ways that harm minority shareholders, and pursue objectives — keeping a plant in the founder's town, preserving a name — that the accounts record as costs.

The reasonable summary is that the form has a characteristic strength and a characteristic weakness that appear at different moments. It is well suited to running a business and badly suited to choosing who runs it next, and the firms that endure across generations are generally those that separated the two questions before the second one arrived.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, family control reduces one cost of ownership because
options: A. family members accept lower salaries
B. such firms are exempt from disclosure requirements
C. banks lend to family firms on better terms
D. an owner who also manages does not need the apparatus that dispersed shareholders require to monitor managers
E. family firms are usually smaller
questions.explanation: The monitoring argument is the first advantage set out, and the passage names boards, disclosure and takeover threats as the expensive alternatives.

questions.passageText:
Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had moved, and assembled evidence of a kind that is now regarded as strong: matching coastlines, matching rock formations across oceans, fossils of the same land species on separated continents, and glacial deposits in what are now tropical regions. The proposal was rejected by most geologists for four decades, and the reason usually given — conservatism — is only part of the story.

The substantive objection was mechanism. Wegener's suggested forces were demonstrably far too weak to move continental rock through oceanic crust, and physicists showed as much. A theory that explains many observations while requiring an impossible mechanism is in genuine difficulty, and the demand for one was legitimate rather than obstructive.

What changed the situation was not better argument about the existing evidence but a new class of measurement, most of it made for other purposes. Wartime and post-war ocean surveys mapped the sea floor and found the mid-ocean ridges; palaeomagnetic work showed that rocks recorded the field direction at their formation and that these directions differed by continent; and the striped magnetic pattern either side of the ridges, symmetric and matching the reversal timescale, indicated that new sea floor was being created and spreading outward.

That supplied the missing mechanism, and it was not the one Wegener proposed: continents do not plough through the ocean floor, they ride on plates that are created and consumed. The episode is often told as vindication of a lone genius. It reads better as an illustration that a correct conclusion supported by an incorrect mechanism is not yet a theory, and that what resolved the dispute came from instruments nobody had built to settle it.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the principal substantive objection to Wegener's proposal was that
options: A. the forces he proposed were far too weak to move continents through oceanic crust
B. his evidence was fabricated
C. matching fossils could be explained by land bridges
D. the continents' coastlines do not in fact match
E. geologists had not surveyed the ocean floor
questions.explanation: The passage calls the demand for a workable mechanism legitimate rather than obstructive.

questions.passageText:
The rapid shift to remote and hybrid work has generated a large empirical literature in a short time, and the findings are less contradictory than the coverage suggests once the questions are separated.

On individual productivity in tasks that can be measured — calls handled, cases processed, code committed — remote work performs comparably to office work and sometimes better, with the gains concentrated in reduced commuting and fewer interruptions. On tasks whose output is harder to observe, the evidence is thinner, and studies relying on self-report or on manager assessment measure something other than output.

The consistent finding concerns not productivity but the transmission of knowledge. Junior employees receive less feedback, and the informal observation by which people learn how work is actually done occurs less. Effects on the individual's current output may be small while the effect on their development is not, and these appear on different timescales, which is why a firm can measure no productivity loss for two years and face one later.

Two further results are robust. Fully remote arrangements and fully office-based ones both lose to hybrid ones on retention, which suggests employees value the option rather than either extreme. And the aggregate effects fall unevenly across places rather than across firms: city-centre economies built around commuter spending face a permanent reduction in demand that no arrangement inside any single firm addresses, and that displacement, rather than any change in output per worker, is the largest measured consequence so far.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that studies of remote work relying on manager assessment
options: A. are the most reliable evidence available
B. apply only to junior employees
C. have not been conducted
D. measure something other than output
E. confirm the findings from measured tasks
questions.explanation: Stated where the passage distinguishes measurable tasks from those whose output is hard to observe.

questions.passageText:
A translation is commonly judged by fidelity, as though the original were a fixed quantity that a translation preserves in greater or lesser proportion. Working translators rarely describe the task that way, and the reason is instructive.

Any text does several things at once. It states something; it does so in a register that positions its speaker; it sounds a particular way; it alludes to what its first readers knew. These properties compete under translation. Preserving a pun may require changing what is said; preserving metre may require a different image; a phrase that was ordinary in its own language becomes conspicuous if rendered literally, so literal fidelity to the words can produce infidelity to the effect.

The translator therefore ranks the properties, and the ranking is a judgement about what the text is for. A legal contract, a liturgy, a comic novel and a technical manual each impose different orders, and a translator who applies one text's ranking to another produces work that is wrong in a way no dictionary will show.

This is why retranslation is normal rather than an admission of earlier failure. Successive translations of a major work are not converging on a correct version; they are making different rankings, often in response to what readers of their moment need explained. The useful question about a translation is not how faithful it is but what it chose to be faithful to — and a translation that never had to choose is describing a text that was doing only one thing.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that literal fidelity to a text's words can produce
options: A. a more accurate rendering of its meaning
B. infidelity to its effect, since an ordinary phrase may become conspicuous
C. a translation suitable for legal purposes only
D. the same ranking of properties as the original
E. a version that requires no retranslation
questions.explanation: The example given is of a phrase ordinary in its own language becoming conspicuous when rendered word for word.

Two further results are robust. Fully remote arrangements and fully office-based ones both lose to hybrid ones on retention, which suggests employees value the option rather than either extreme. And the aggregate effects fall unevenly across places rather than across firms: city-centre economies built around commuter spending face a permanent reduction in demand that no arrangement inside any single firm addresses, and that displacement, rather than any change in output per worker, is the largest measured consequence so far.

readingPassages.title: What Survives Translation
readingPassages.text:
A translation is commonly judged by fidelity, as though the original were a fixed quantity that a translation preserves in greater or lesser proportion. Working translators rarely describe the task that way, and the reason is instructive.

Any text does several things at once. It states something; it does so in a register that positions its speaker; it sounds a particular way; it alludes to what its first readers knew. These properties compete under translation. Preserving a pun may require changing what is said; preserving metre may require a different image; a phrase that was ordinary in its own language becomes conspicuous if rendered literally, so literal fidelity to the words can produce infidelity to the effect.

The translator therefore ranks the properties, and the ranking is a judgement about what the text is for. A legal contract, a liturgy, a comic novel and a technical manual each impose different orders, and a translator who applies one text's ranking to another produces work that is wrong in a way no dictionary will show.

This is why retranslation is normal rather than an admission of earlier failure. Successive translations of a major work are not converging on a correct version; they are making different rankings, often in response to what readers of their moment need explained. The useful question about a translation is not how faithful it is but what it chose to be faithful to — and a translation that never had to choose is describing a text that was doing only one thing.
